newsitem.title: GERMANY: BDI says Germany moves further away from jobs goal.
newsitem.headline: BDI says Germany moves further away from jobs goal.

text.p: Germany has wasted a year as unemployment mounts to record levels, leaving it farther from its goal of halving joblessness by 2000, Federation of German Industry (BDI) president Hans Olaf Henkel said on Tuesday.
"The chances of creating two million new jobs by the year 2000 are now much slimmer than they were a year ago," Henkel told reporters. "We have lost at least a year on the labour market."
Still, Henkel said he stands by the goal, because Germany was able to create three million jobs in a similar time in the 1980s, he said.

Unemployment rose above 4.1 million in December from 3.8 million a year earlier, and appears to be heading upward. The high cost of Germany's social welfare state remains the main obstacle to progress on the jobs front, he said.
Policy makers are moving in the right direction, but the pace of reform is too slow. "Tax policy must remain fixed on the goal of doing everything possible to make it easier to create jobs," he said.
The government, which now accounts for every second mark spent in Germany, must strive harder to reduce its share of the economy to 45.8 percent, the level before unification, he said.
Some tax cuts sought by industry have been realised, but others, including the reduction in the unpopular solidarity surcharge on income taxes, have been postponed or blocked.
"The new burdens on industry in the past year have outweighed the burdens that have been removed," he said, adding that this has forced up both corporate insolvencies and unemployment.
Henkel sought to deflect criticism that industry, which has remained reluctant to invest despite the economic upturn over the past year, is dragging its feet on jobs initiatives.

"Companies need investment conditions that give them a chance to make money," he said. "They need motivated employees, enough capital, and orders for products and services at competitive quality and costs."

Henkel rejected Chancellor Helmut Kohl's suggestion that companies could create new jobs by slashing overtime. He said it was not clear yet whether Kohl would convene a new round of talks involving labour, management and government, reviving last year's failed "Alliance for Jobs".
Germany needs to cut taxes under planned reforms to bring taxation in line with competing countries, as well as reform its industrial pay bargaining system to increase flexibility, he said.

Germany could learn much from the United States' flexible labour market, recent sharp cuts in corporate taxes in Britain, Austria and Sweden, deregulation in New Zealand and economic reforms in Ireland, he said.
